answers: Run the instance in an Auto Scaling group with min/max/desired capacity of 1 spanning multiple AZs
Front the instance with a load balancer health check so failures are detected at the application level
explanation: A "min 1, max 1" ASG is the self-healing pattern for stateful singletons: when the instance or its AZ dies, the ASG launches a replacement in a surviving AZ. The load balancer adds application-level health detection (and a stable endpoint while the instance is replaced). The exam guide calls this out as improving reliability "when application changes are not possible" — refactoring violates the constraint, and reboots/resizing don't address failures.

question: A developer accidentally ran a destructive UPDATE against production RDS at 14:32. The database has automated backups with 7-day retention. What is the best recovery option?
options: Point-in-time restore to a new instance at 14:31 and recover the affected data
Reboot the instance to roll back uncommitted transactions
Restore last night's manual snapshot over the current instance
Enable Multi-AZ and fail over to the standby
answer: Point-in-time restore to a new instance at 14:31 and recover the affected data
explanation: Automated backups combine daily snapshots with continuous transaction logs, allowing restore to any second within retention (up to the last ~5 minutes). PITR creates a *new* instance at the chosen moment — you then copy the affected rows back, losing only what changed in one minute. A reboot can't undo committed writes; last night's snapshot discards a full day; the Multi-AZ standby faithfully replicated the bad UPDATE too — replication is not a backup.

question: An Auto Scaling group has 8 instances in AZ-a and 2 in AZ-b behind a load balancer. Users report inconsistent performance — instances in AZ-b receive far more traffic per instance. What balances the per-instance load?
options: Enable cross-zone load balancing so traffic distributes evenly across all instances regardless of AZ
Add more instances to AZ-b manually
Switch the ALB to least-connections routing
Create a separate load balancer per AZ
answer: Enable cross-zone load balancing so traffic distributes evenly across all instances regardless of AZ
explanation: Without cross-zone load balancing, each load balancer node splits traffic 50/50 between AZs — so AZ-b's 2 instances share the same half that AZ-a's 8 share, getting 4× the per-instance load. Cross-zone distributes across all 10 instances equally. It's on by default for ALB but *off* by default for NLB — a favorite exam detail. The other options treat symptoms or add complexity.

question: When orders change status, several systems (email, analytics, inventory, plus future additions) must react — each filtering for only the event types it cares about. The order service should not know its consumers. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon EventBridge with rules routing filtered events to each target
Direct SDK calls from the order service to each downstream system
A shared database table that consumers poll for changes
An SQS queue that all systems read from
answer: Amazon EventBridge with rules routing filtered events to each target
explanation: EventBridge is the event bus for exactly this: producers publish once, rules pattern-match event content and route to many targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, APIs), and new consumers mean a new rule — the producer never changes. Direct calls couple the producer to every consumer; polling a table adds latency and load; one shared SQS queue delivers each message to a single consumer, not to all of them.

question: A company must apply one consistent backup policy — daily backups, 35-day retention, copies to a second Region — across its EBS volumes, RDS databases, DynamoDB tables, and EFS file systems, with compliance reporting. Which service does this centrally?
options: AWS Backup with a backup plan assigned to tagged resources
Separate snapshot scripts per service triggered by cron
S3 lifecycle rules
AWS Config
answer: AWS Backup with a backup plan assigned to tagged resources
explanation: AWS Backup is the single control plane for backups across a dozen-plus services: plans define schedule/retention/cross-Region copy, resources join by tag or ARN, vaults can be locked (WORM), and audit reporting is built in. Per-service scripts are exactly the sprawl it replaces; S3 lifecycle manages storage classes of existing objects; Config records configuration, not data.

question: A marketing site is fully static (HTML, CSS, JS, images). It currently runs on one EC2 instance, which has failed twice during campaigns. Which combination gives the site the highest availability with the LEAST operational effort? (Select TWO)
options: Host the static files in Amazon S3 with static website hosting
Serve the site through an Amazon CloudFront distribution
Move the site to a larger EC2 instance with daily AMI backups
Run nginx on two EC2 instances behind an ALB
Store the files on an EFS volume mounted to the existing instance
answers: Host the static files in Amazon S3 with static website hosting
Serve the site through an Amazon CloudFront distribution
explanation: Static content needs no servers at all: S3 provides 11-nines durable, regionally redundant hosting, and CloudFront adds global caching, HTTPS, and absorbs traffic spikes. Nothing to patch, no instances to fail — strictly more available than any EC2 arrangement and cheaper too. The EC2/EFS options keep operating servers to serve files that don't need one.

question: A trading platform sees a massive, predictable traffic spike every weekday at exactly 9:00 AM when markets open. Dynamic scaling reacts too slowly, causing 10 minutes of degraded service. What should the architect add?
options: A scheduled scaling action that increases desired capacity shortly before 9:00 AM on weekdays
A higher CPU threshold on the existing target tracking policy
Smaller instances so they launch faster
A second metric alarm on memory usage
answer: A scheduled scaling action that increases desired capacity shortly before 9:00 AM on weekdays
explanation: Reactive policies by definition scale *after* load arrives — boot plus warm-up time creates the 10-minute gap. For a known schedule, scheduled actions pre-provision capacity (e.g. at 8:45) so instances are in service when the spike hits; predictive scaling is the ML alternative when the pattern is regular but not clock-exact. Threshold and metric tweaks still react after the fact.

question: An application calling AWS APIs occasionally receives ThrottlingException errors during bursts. Retrying immediately makes the problem worse. What is the AWS-recommended client-side pattern?
options: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
Retrying in a tight loop until the call succeeds
Catching and ignoring the throttling errors
Switching all API calls to a single sequential worker permanently
answer: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
explanation: Exponential backoff spreads retries out (1s, 2s, 4s…) so a throttled fleet doesn't immediately re-stampede the API, and jitter (randomization) prevents synchronized retry waves from clients that were throttled together. AWS SDKs implement this by default. Tight loops amplify throttling; ignoring errors drops work; permanent serialization sacrifices throughput to avoid a transient condition.

question: A critical public API must keep working even if its entire primary AWS Region fails. Which combination of actions provides Regional failover? (Select TWO)
options: Deploy a full copy of the API stack in a second Region
Use Route 53 failover routing with health checks to switch DNS to the second Region when the primary fails
Add more Availability Zones to the existing Region's deployment
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the existing ALB
Increase the existing Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity
answers: Deploy a full copy of the API stack in a second Region
Use Route 53 failover routing with health checks to switch DNS to the second Region when the primary fails
explanation: Region-level resilience needs two things: a stack that exists somewhere else (warm standby or active-active in Region 2, with data replicated), and a traffic-steering mechanism that notices the failure and redirects — Route 53 failover records with health checks (or Global Accelerator endpoint failover). More AZs, cross-zone balancing, and bigger ASGs all harden *within* the Region that just failed.

question: An application is deployed in three Regions. Every user should be routed to the Region that gives THEM the fastest response, and unhealthy Regions must be taken out of rotation automatically. Which Route 53 configuration fits?
options: Latency-based routing records with health checks on each Regional endpoint
Geolocation routing mapping each continent to a fixed Region
A failover policy with one primary and two secondaries
Simple records returning all three Regional IPs
answer: Latency-based routing records with health checks on each Regional endpoint
explanation: Latency-based routing answers each DNS query with the Region that has the lowest measured network latency for that user — not necessarily the geographically nearest — and health checks remove failing Regions from consideration. Geolocation is for compliance/content localization (fixed mapping, even when slow); failover is active-passive, wasting two Regions; simple records do no steering and no health awareness.

question: A gaming company needs an in-memory store for real-time leaderboards (sorted rankings), with replication and automatic failover for high availability, plus persistence options. Which engine should they choose?
options: ElastiCache for Redis
ElastiCache for Memcached
DynamoDB standard tables
RDS MySQL with a large buffer pool
answer: ElastiCache for Redis
explanation: The requirements map to Redis features: sorted sets are purpose-built for leaderboards, and Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, snapshots/AOF persistence, and pub/sub. Memcached is the simpler engine — multithreaded and easy to scale out, but no replication, persistence, or rich data structures. The Redis-vs-Memcached feature split is a reliable exam question.

question: A DynamoDB table uses `status` (values: ACTIVE, INACTIVE) as its partition key. The table is heavily throttled even though provisioned capacity far exceeds total traffic. What is the root cause?
options: The low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic on one or two partitions (hot partitions), exceeding per-partition limits
DynamoDB tables require a sort key to scale
The table needs a global secondary index to spread load
Provisioned capacity applies per item, not per table
answer: The low-cardinality partition key concentrates traffic on one or two partitions (hot partitions), exceeding per-partition limits
explanation: DynamoDB spreads data and throughput across partitions by hashing the partition key. With only two possible values, virtually all traffic lands on two partitions — each capped at 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU — so the table throttles while aggregate capacity sits idle. The fix is a high-cardinality key (user ID, order ID), possibly with write sharding. Sort keys and GSIs don't repair a degenerate partition key choice.

question: Consumers poll an SQS queue continuously. Most ReceiveMessage calls return empty, driving up API costs and CPU. What is the recommended fix?
options: Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
Poll less frequently with a 5-minute sleep between calls
Switch to a FIFO queue
Increase the visibility timeout
answer: Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
explanation: Long polling holds the ReceiveMessage call open (up to 20 s) until a message arrives or the wait expires — eliminating the empty-response storm, cutting API calls (cost) dramatically, and *reducing* delivery latency versus sleeping between polls. Five-minute sleeps add up to 5 minutes of latency; FIFO changes ordering semantics; visibility timeout governs in-flight message invisibility, not polling behavior.

question: A customer-facing API built on Lambda shows occasional latency spikes of 1–2 seconds on the first request after idle periods, while typical requests take 50 ms. Which feature removes these spikes?
options: Provisioned concurrency on the function's production alias
A larger memory allocation
Reserved concurrency
Moving the function code to a container image
answer: Provisioned concurrency on the function's production alias
explanation: The spikes are cold starts — initializing a new execution environment. Provisioned concurrency keeps a configured number of environments initialized and warm, so requests hit pre-warmed instances at steady latency. More memory speeds execution but doesn't prevent initialization; *reserved* concurrency is a limit/guarantee on concurrent executions (a different knob with a confusingly similar name — classic exam distractor); container images generally cold-start slower, not faster.

question: A machine-learning team runs distributed training on hundreds of EC2 instances that need a shared POSIX file system with sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s of aggregate throughput, sourcing training data from S3. Which storage service fits?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre with an S3-linked data repository
Amazon EFS Standard
Amazon S3 mounted via Mountpoint on each node
A large gp3 EBS volume attached to the head node and shared over NFS
answer: Amazon FSx for Lustre with an S3-linked data repository
explanation: FSx for Lustre is the HPC/ML file system: parallel architecture delivering hundreds of GB/s and sub-millisecond latencies, with data repository association that lazy-loads from and writes back to S3. EFS is general-purpose NFS — solid, but not in Lustre's performance class for this pattern. Mountpoint for S3 suits sequential object access, not POSIX random I/O; one instance re-exporting an EBS volume bottlenecks the entire cluster.

question: A company is moving a Windows application that requires shared SMB file storage with Active Directory integration and NTFS permissions. Which AWS service provides this?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EFS
Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Lustre
answer: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
explanation: FSx for Windows is a fully managed native Windows file system: SMB protocol, NTFS, DFS namespaces, and AD integration (AWS managed AD or self-managed). EFS speaks NFS — Linux territory; S3 is object storage, not a file share; FSx for Lustre targets Linux HPC. The protocol is the tell: SMB/AD → FSx for Windows, NFS/Linux → EFS, parallel HPC → Lustre.

question: Application logs must be streamed into S3 (and optionally Redshift) in near real time, with optional transformation via Lambda — and the team wants zero servers, shards, or consumer applications to manage. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom consumer
Amazon SQS with a fleet of worker instances
AWS DataSync on a schedule
answer: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
explanation: Firehose is the fully managed delivery pipe: it batches, optionally transforms (Lambda) and converts formats, and delivers to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and third parties — no shards to size, no consumers to write, scaling handled. Kinesis Data Streams is the answer when you need custom real-time consumers or replay; SQS+workers is hand-built plumbing; DataSync moves file systems, not streams. "Easiest way to load streaming data into X" → Firehose.

question: Analysts run complex aggregation queries joining billions of rows of sales history for BI dashboards. The current RDS PostgreSQL instance takes minutes per query. Which service is purpose-built for this workload?
options: Amazon Redshift
A larger RDS PostgreSQL instance
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon ElastiCache
answer: Amazon Redshift
explanation: This is OLAP — scanning and aggregating huge datasets — and Redshift's columnar storage, compression, and massively parallel processing are built for it, routinely turning minutes into seconds at petabyte scale. RDS is row-oriented OLTP; scaling it up delays the wall. DynamoDB serves key-based access patterns, not ad-hoc joins; ElastiCache accelerates repeated reads, not novel analytical queries. OLTP→RDS, OLAP→Redshift is core exam vocabulary.

question: An e-commerce site needs product search with full-text queries, fuzzy matching for typos, filters, and relevance ranking. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon RDS with LIKE queries
Amazon DynamoDB with scan operations
Amazon Athena
answer: Amazon OpenSearch Service
explanation: OpenSearch (the Elasticsearch fork) is the managed search engine: inverted indexes for full-text search, fuzzy matching, faceted filtering, and relevance scoring out of the box. SQL `LIKE '%term%'` can't use indexes and offers no ranking; DynamoDB scans are expensive table reads with no text awareness; Athena is batch SQL over S3, not an interactive search backend.

question: A tightly coupled simulation across a fleet of EC2 instances is bottlenecked by inter-node network latency and throughput. Which combination of changes improves node-to-node network performance? (Select TWO)
options: Use instance types with enhanced networking (ENA) and high network bandwidth
Launch the fleet in a cluster placement group in one AZ
Spread the instances across three Regions for more total bandwidth
Attach larger EBS volumes to every node
Put an Application Load Balancer between the nodes
answers: Use instance types with enhanced networking (ENA) and high network bandwidth
Launch the fleet in a cluster placement group in one AZ
explanation: Two complementary levers: enhanced networking (ENA, and EFA for MPI-style HPC) raises per-instance packet rates and lowers latency, while a cluster placement group physically co-locates the fleet on a low-latency, high-bisection network segment. Spreading across Regions multiplies latency by orders of magnitude; EBS is storage, not network; an ALB is an HTTP front door, not an inter-node fabric.

question: An Aurora cluster has one writer and four read replicas. The application should spread its read queries across all replicas automatically, including ones added later by replica auto scaling. What should the application connect to?
options: The cluster's reader endpoint
The cluster endpoint
Each replica's instance endpoint, in rotation managed by application code
The writer's IP address
answer: The cluster's reader endpoint
explanation: Aurora's reader endpoint load-balances connections across all current read replicas — replicas added or removed by auto scaling join and leave automatically, no application changes. The cluster endpoint always targets the writer (use it for writes); hand-rolled rotation over instance endpoints breaks every time the replica set changes; raw IPs break on failover.

question: A REST API on API Gateway serves catalog data that changes every few minutes. Identical GET requests hammer the Lambda backend thousands of times per minute. What reduces backend load with minimal changes?
options: Enable API Gateway caching on the stage with a TTL of a few minutes
Raise the Lambda reserved concurrency
Move the API to a larger Lambda memory size
Switch the integration from Lambda to EC2
answer: Enable API Gateway caching on the stage with a TTL of a few minutes
explanation: Stage-level caching stores responses keyed by request (configurable per method and by parameters), serving repeats from cache until the TTL expires — the Lambda invocation count collapses, which also cuts cost. Matching the TTL to the data's change cadence (a few minutes) keeps staleness acceptable. More concurrency or memory just processes the redundant invocations faster; changing compute doesn't remove the redundancy.

question: A data-processing job needs scratch space with millions of IOPS and microsecond latency for temporary intermediate files that are worthless after the job completes. Which storage offers the highest performance for this?
options: NVMe instance store volumes on a storage-optimized instance family
An io2 EBS volume with maximum provisioned IOPS
Amazon EFS with provisioned throughput
Amazon S3 with multipart uploads
answer: NVMe instance store volumes on a storage-optimized instance family
explanation: Instance store is physically attached NVMe — no network hop — delivering millions of IOPS and microsecond latency that even io2 Block Express (network-attached) can't match. Its catch is ephemerality: data is lost on stop/termination, which is exactly acceptable for scratch files. The exam pattern: "temporary/scratch/cache + extreme IOPS" → instance store; "persistent + high IOPS" → io2.

question: An application caches database results in ElastiCache using lazy loading (cache-aside) only. Users complain that data is sometimes stale for a long time after updates. Adding which caching strategy keeps the cache current while preserving fast reads?
options: Write-through — update the cache at the same time the database is written
A shorter connection timeout to the cache
Caching the misses as well as the hits
Switching from Redis to Memcached
answer: Write-through — update the cache at the same time the database is written
explanation: Lazy loading populates the cache only on read misses, so an updated row stays stale until its cached copy expires. Write-through complements it: every database write also updates the cache, so reads always see current data. The classic combination is write-through plus lazy loading with a TTL as a safety net — TTLs bound staleness for anything written by paths that bypass the cache. The other options change failure behavior, memory usage, or engine, not freshness.

question: A new application's DynamoDB traffic is completely unpredictable — hours of near-zero activity, then sudden unannounced spikes. Which capacity mode is MOST cost-effective and operationally simple?
options: On-demand capacity mode — pay per request with no capacity planning
Provisioned capacity sized for the largest possible spike
Provisioned capacity with auto scaling and aggressive targets
Reserved capacity purchased for three years
answer: On-demand capacity mode — pay per request with no capacity planning
explanation: On-demand bills per million requests and absorbs sudden spikes without pre-provisioning — near-zero idle hours cost near zero. Provisioning for peak pays for the spike 24/7; auto scaling reacts in minutes, so unannounced spikes throttle first; reserved capacity commits to a baseline this workload doesn't have. The crossover: steady, predictable traffic eventually makes provisioned cheaper — the exam tests recognizing which side you're on.

question: An S3 bill shows significant storage charges that don't match the visible objects in the bucket. The bucket receives many large uploads from unreliable clients. What hidden cost is likely, and how is it fixed?
options: Abandoned incomplete multipart uploads — add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload
Delete markers from versioning — disable versioning
S3 access logs stored in the same bucket — disable logging
Cross-Region replication copies — delete the replica bucket
answer: Abandoned incomplete multipart uploads — add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload
explanation: Parts of a multipart upload that's never completed or aborted sit invisibly — they don't appear in object listings but bill as storage indefinitely. Unreliable clients abandoning large uploads accumulate them fast. The lifecycle rule `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` (e.g. after 7 days) cleans them automatically; Storage Lens and `ListMultipartUploads` reveal the backlog. The other options describe costs that are visible or intentional.

question: A containerized Linux workload runs on m5 (x86) instances. The team wants better price-performance with minimal changes. Which option typically delivers up to ~40% better price-performance?
options: Migrate to Graviton (ARM-based) instances such as m7g after rebuilding images for arm64
Upgrade to the newest x86 generation at the same size
Move every workload to t3.micro instances
Switch the containers to Windows hosts
answer: Migrate to Graviton (ARM-based) instances such as m7g after rebuilding images for arm64
explanation: Graviton instances are AWS's headline price-performance lever — up to 40% better than comparable x86 — and containerized Linux workloads are the easiest migration: rebuild multi-arch images, redeploy. Newer x86 generations help single-digit percentages; t3.micro is a size, not a strategy (undersizing causes throttling); Windows adds license cost. Watch for the constraint in questions: closed-source x86-only binaries block the move.

question: A development VPC has private subnets in three AZs, each with its own NAT gateway. The dev workloads tolerate downtime. What reduces NAT costs?
options: Consolidate to a single NAT gateway shared by all three AZs, accepting the availability trade-off
Replace the NAT gateways with internet gateways in each private subnet
Add a fourth NAT gateway for redundancy
Move all workloads to public subnets with public IPs
answer: Consolidate to a single NAT gateway shared by all three AZs, accepting the availability trade-off
explanation: Each NAT gateway bills hourly (~$32/month) plus per-GB processing; three of them triple the hourly cost. Dev environments that tolerate downtime can route all private subnets to one NAT gateway — the documented cost optimization, with the explicit trade-off that an AZ failure breaks egress for the others (which is why production keeps one per AZ, plus avoiding cross-AZ data charges). Internet gateways don't provide NAT for private instances; public IPs change the security posture.

question: A popular site serves large downloads directly from S3 to the internet, generating big data-transfer-out charges. How can delivery cost be reduced while improving download speed?
options: Serve the downloads through CloudFront — S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and edge delivery rates are lower
Compress all files into ZIP archives
Move the bucket to a cheaper Region and keep serving directly
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the downloads
answer: Serve the downloads through CloudFront — S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and edge delivery rates are lower
explanation: Origin-to-CloudFront transfer is free, CloudFront's per-GB internet rates undercut S3's, caching means popular files leave the origin once instead of millions of times, and users download from nearby edges — cheaper *and* faster. Compression helps but doesn't change rates; Region arbitrage saves cents while adding latency; Transfer Acceleration is for *uploads* and adds cost.

question: A high-volume Lambda function dominates the monthly serverless bill. The code is already efficient. Which combination of changes reduces its cost without rewriting the logic? (Select TWO)
options: Migrate the function to arm64 (Graviton), which is billed about 20% cheaper per ms
Tune the memory setting to the sweet spot using power tuning, since billing is memory × duration
Increase the timeout to the 15-minute maximum
Switch the function to provisioned concurrency at all hours
Invoke the function more frequently with smaller payloads
answers: Migrate the function to arm64 (Graviton), which is billed about 20% cheaper per ms
Tune the memory setting to the sweet spot using power tuning, since billing is memory × duration
explanation: Lambda bills GB-seconds: arm64 cuts the per-ms price (~20%) and often runs faster too, while memory tuning finds the point where added CPU shortens duration enough to lower memory × time (tools like Lambda Power Tuning automate the sweep — sometimes *more* memory is cheaper). Timeout is a safety cap, not a billing factor; always-on provisioned concurrency *adds* an hourly charge; more invocations means more request fees and per-invocation overhead.

question: A company must restore 500 TB from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for a regulatory review due in one week. Cost matters more than speed. Which retrieval option should they use?
options: Bulk retrieval — the cheapest tier, completing within 5–12 hours
Expedited retrieval for every archive
Standard retrieval with provisioned capacity units
Copy the archives to S3 Standard first, then download
answer: Bulk retrieval — the cheapest tier, completing within 5–12 hours
explanation: Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers three tiers: expedited (1–5 min, most expensive), standard (3–5 h), and bulk (5–12 h, lowest cost — designed exactly for large planned restores like this). A week of lead time makes bulk's window irrelevant. Expedited at 500 TB maximizes spend for unneeded speed; provisioned capacity exists to guarantee *expedited* throughput; "copy first" still performs a retrieval underneath.

question: Internal tools average 5% CPU with occasional brief bursts to 60%. They currently run on m5.large instances. Which instance family is designed for this usage pattern at lower cost?
options: T family burstable instances (e.g. t3.large), which accrue CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts
C family compute-optimized instances
R family memory-optimized instances
P family GPU instances
answer: T family burstable instances (e.g. t3.large), which accrue CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts
explanation: Burstable instances price for a low CPU baseline and bank credits during idle time to spend on bursts — a 5%-average workload runs comfortably and costs notably less than the equivalent m5. Watch the failure mode (also exam-tested): sustained high CPU drains credits and throttles to baseline, unless `unlimited` mode is on — which can quietly cost more than a fixed-performance instance.

question: A fault-tolerant processing fleet runs on Spot Instances of a single instance type and suffers frequent simultaneous interruptions when that capacity pool gets reclaimed. What reduces both interruptions and cost?
options: Use an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy diversifying across many instance types and AZs, with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
Bid a higher maximum price for the same single instance type
Switch the whole fleet to On-Demand
Run all Spot instances in one AZ to keep them together
answer: Use an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy diversifying across many instance types and AZs, with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy
explanation: Spot interruptions happen per capacity pool (instance type × AZ). Diversifying across many pools means a single pool's reclamation takes out only a slice of the fleet, and the capacity-optimized strategy launches into the deepest pools, statistically reducing interruptions. "Bidding" higher doesn't help — the strategy is capacity-driven, and you pay the Spot market price regardless. Full On-Demand forfeits the ~90% savings; concentrating in one AZ is maximum blast radius.

question: Thousands of EBS snapshots accumulate from years of ad-hoc backups, inflating storage costs. The policy should be: daily snapshots, retain 14 days, then delete — automatically. Which service implements this?
options: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) snapshot policies
A reminder for engineers to clean up monthly
S3 lifecycle rules applied to the snapshots
AWS Trusted Advisor automated deletion
answer: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) snapshot policies
explanation: DLM automates EBS snapshot (and AMI) lifecycles: tag-targeted policies create snapshots on schedule and expire them by age or count — exactly "daily, keep 14, delete". (AWS Backup is the broader alternative when one plan must span multiple services.) S3 lifecycle rules don't govern EBS snapshots even though snapshots live in S3 internally; Trusted Advisor reports, it doesn't delete; manual cleanup is how the problem grew.

question: A monthly cost review should automatically surface idle and underused resources — unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers, underutilized EC2 instances — with concrete recommendations. Which TWO tools provide these findings? (Select TWO)
options: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Compute Optimizer rightsizing recommendations
AWS CloudTrail event history
Amazon Route 53 health checks
AWS Artifact reports
answers: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
AWS Compute Optimizer rightsizing recommendations
explanation: Trusted Advisor's cost checks flag idle resources — unassociated Elastic IPs, idle load balancers, low-utilization instances, unattached volumes. Compute Optimizer goes deeper on sizing: ML over CloudWatch metrics yields specific instance-type recommendations (also for EBS, Lambda, ECS). Together they cover "what's wasted" and "what's oversized". CloudTrail is an API audit log; Route 53 checks endpoint health; Artifact downloads compliance documents.

question: Non-production RDS instances (dev, test, staging) run 24/7 but are only used during business hours on weekdays. Snapshots must be retained. What is the simplest cost reduction?
options: Stop the instances outside business hours (e.g. with an automated scheduler), since stopped instances don't incur instance-hours
Delete the instances every evening and recreate them each morning from scratch
Convert them all to Multi-AZ for efficiency
Move them to io2 storage
answer: Stop the instances outside business hours (e.g. with an automated scheduler), since stopped instances don't incur instance-hours
explanation: Stopped RDS instances stop billing instance-hours (storage and backups still bill) — nights and weekends cut runtime ~75%. Caveat worth knowing: RDS auto-starts stopped instances after 7 days, so schedulers re-stop them. Delete/recreate loses configuration and takes time daily; Multi-AZ *doubles* instance cost; io2 raises storage cost. Pair with right-sizing for the remaining hours.
